questions.question: In a binary search tree (BST), for any node, which property must hold?

BFS always visits fewer vertices than DFS

By checking whether any vertex has degree greater than 2

A cycle exists if DFS ever revisits any previously visited vertex, exactly as in the undirected case
A cycle exists only if the graph has more edges than vertices
Directed graphs can never contain cycles, so no such check is needed
questions.explanation: In directed graphs, an edge to a vertex visited earlier but no longer on the current DFS path (already finished) is a legitimate cross or forward edge, not a cycle; only an edge back to an ancestor still on the recursion stack closes an actual cycle, which is why directed cycle detection tracks an explicit 'on-stack' set in addition to a 'visited' set.

questions.explanation: A bubble sort that stops early when a full pass makes no swaps runs in O(n) on an already-sorted array, since one pass confirms no swaps are needed; on a reverse-sorted array it needs Theta(n^2) comparisons and swaps across n passes.

Theta(n^2) comparisons and Theta(n^2) swaps

options: Best-case O(n) for nearly/already sorted input; worst-case O(n^2) for reverse-sorted input
Best-case O(n log n); worst-case O(n log n)
Best-case O(1); worst-case O(n)
Best-case and worst-case are both O(n^2), regardless of input order

questions.question: Merge sort is described as stable and as requiring O(n) auxiliary space. What in its algorithm produces each of those two properties?
options: Stability comes from the merge step always taking from the left sub-array first when keys are equal; the O(n) space comes from needing a temporary array to hold merged output before copying it back
Stability comes from sorting in place with no extra memory; the O(n) space is only used for the recursion call stack
It is not actually stable; the O(n) space is for storing the pivot at each level
Stability and the O(n) space are both consequences of always splitting the array exactly in half

questions.question: Quicksort that always picks the first element of the (sub)array as the pivot is run on an already-sorted array of n elements. What time complexity results, and why?
options: O(n^2), because each partition splits off only a single element (the pivot ends up at one extreme every time), leaving a recursive call on n-1 elements at every level
O(n log n), the same as the average case, because pivot choice never affects quicksort's complexity
O(n), because a sorted array requires no swaps
O(log n), because sorted input always produces perfectly balanced partitions
questions.explanation: On sorted input, taking the first element as pivot means every one of the remaining n-1 elements is larger, so the partition is maximally unbalanced (1 element versus n-1); the recurrence T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n) solves to O(n^2), quicksort's classic worst case, which is why practical implementations use randomized or median-of-three pivot selection to avoid this pattern on sorted or adversarial input.

questions.question: Why is 'median-of-three' (comparing the first, middle, and last elements and using their median) a commonly used pivot-selection strategy for quicksort?
options: It is cheap to compute, O(1), yet substantially reduces the chance of consistently picking an extreme value as pivot, avoiding the worst-case O(n^2) pattern on already-sorted or reverse-sorted input
It guarantees O(n log n) worst-case time in every situation
It eliminates the need for a partition step entirely
It always selects the true median of the entire array in O(1) time
questions.explanation: Median-of-three does not guarantee balance in every adversarial case, since an adversary can still construct bad inputs, but it is a cheap heuristic that is far less likely to hit the worst-case pattern than always using the first or last element, precisely the pathological case for already-sorted arrays.

questions.question: Counting sort achieves O(n+k) time, with n elements and k possible key values, instead of the Omega(n log n) comparison-sort lower bound. How does it do this, and what limits its applicability?
options: It counts occurrences of each key value directly, never comparing two elements against each other, and uses those counts to place elements, so it works well only when k is not much larger than n and keys are small non-negative integers (or can be mapped to them)
It uses a smarter comparison strategy that halves the search space each step, and works on any comparable data type
It is a comparison sort that happens to run faster than merge sort on all inputs
It sorts by recursively partitioning around a pivot, the same as quicksort, but with a different pivot rule
questions.explanation: Because it never compares two elements directly, counting sort sidesteps the Omega(n log n) comparison-sort lower bound entirely, but this only pays off when the key range k is small, ideally O(n); for a very large or non-integer key range it becomes impractical or inapplicable.

O(n log n) regardless of d
O(n+k) regardless of d

The input must already be nearly sorted before bucket sort is applied
The number of buckets must equal n^2
It achieves O(n) time for any input distribution, including highly skewed ones

questions.question: Comparison-based sorting algorithms, those that only compare pairs of elements such as merge sort or quicksort, have a worst-case lower bound of Omega(n log n) comparisons. What argument establishes this bound?
options: A decision-tree argument: there are n! possible orderings of n elements, and a binary decision tree distinguishing all of them needs at least log2(n!) = Omega(n log n) levels, hence comparisons, in the worst case
It follows directly from the master theorem applied to any sort's recurrence
It is an empirical observation with no formal proof
It applies only to merge sort, not to comparison sorts in general
questions.explanation: Since a comparison sort must distinguish among all n! possible input permutations using yes/no comparisons, and a binary tree with n! leaves needs height at least log2(n!), which is Theta(n log n) by Stirling's approximation, no comparison-based algorithm can beat Theta(n log n) in the worst case -- which is exactly why non-comparison sorts like counting sort can only beat it by exploiting extra structure, such as a bounded key range, rather than comparisons.

options: In-place-ness (auxiliary space usage) -- quicksort typically needs only O(log n) extra space for recursion, while standard array-based merge sort needs O(n) extra space
Only merge sort can sort arrays; quicksort only works on linked lists
Quicksort is always slower than merge sort in every case
Merge sort is in-place while quicksort requires extra memory
questions.explanation: Quicksort partitions elements within the same array using swaps, needing only O(log n) stack space for recursion in the balanced case; merge sort's merge step needs a temporary array of size n to combine two sorted runs before copying back, which is why the standard array implementation is described as not in-place.

questions.question: For an array that is already 'nearly sorted', where each element is at most a small constant distance from its final sorted position, which classic comparison sort typically performs best in practice, and why?
options: Insertion sort, because it is adaptive -- its running time is proportional to the number of inversions, which is small for nearly-sorted input
Selection sort, because it always does the same Theta(n^2) comparisons regardless of input order
Merge sort, because it always splits the array exactly in half regardless of existing order
Radix sort, because digit-based sorting ignores existing order entirely
questions.explanation: Insertion sort's inner loop only shifts elements past out-of-place predecessors, so its running time scales with the number of inversions (out-of-order pairs) rather than always doing Theta(n^2) work; a nearly-sorted array has few inversions, making insertion sort close to O(n) in practice, unlike selection sort, which always scans the full remainder.

questions.question: Shell sort generalizes insertion sort by first sorting elements that are far apart, using a decreasing sequence of gaps, and gradually reducing the gap to 1. What is the motivation for this approach?
options: Moving elements long distances early, while the gap is large, removes many inversions cheaply, so the final gap-1 pass (plain insertion sort) has much less work left to do than plain insertion sort would starting from the unsorted array
It guarantees O(n log n) worst-case time, strictly better than plain insertion sort
It eliminates the need for any comparisons in the final pass
It is only used to sort linked lists, never arrays
questions.explanation: Plain insertion sort only ever swaps adjacent elements, so an element far from its correct position must be moved one step at a time; sorting with large gaps first lets far-apart out-of-place elements jump most of the way to their correct position quickly, so by the time the gap shrinks to 1 the array is already close to sorted and the final pass is fast.

options: O(n)
O(n log n)
O(log n)
questions.explanation: Merging advances a pointer through each sub-array, always outputting the smaller of the two current front elements, doing exactly one comparison-and-copy per output position, so a merge of two sub-arrays totaling n elements takes O(n) time; it is the O(log n) levels of recursion, each doing O(n) merge work, that together give merge sort's overall O(n log n).

questions.question: For sorting a singly linked list, with no random access to arbitrary indices, why is merge sort generally preferred over quicksort?
options: Merge sort's merge step only needs sequential access and can be implemented with O(1) extra space for linked lists by relinking pointers, while quicksort's partitioning benefits heavily from random access and tends to degrade without it
Quicksort cannot be implemented on linked lists under any circumstances
Merge sort is not comparison-based, so it avoids the Omega(n log n) lower bound on linked lists
Linked lists cannot be sorted by any O(n log n) algorithm
questions.explanation: Quicksort's efficient in-place partitioning relies on being able to jump directly to arbitrary indices from both ends, which a singly linked list does not support without extra traversal cost; merge sort's merge step only ever needs to look at the current front of each list, so it adapts naturally to sequential-access structures and can even avoid the O(n) auxiliary array needed for array-based merging by relinking nodes in place.

questions.question: 'External sorting' refers to sorting techniques used when the dataset is too large to fit in main memory. What general strategy do external sorting algorithms, such as external merge sort, use?
options: Break the data into chunks small enough to fit in memory, sort each chunk internally, write the sorted chunks (runs) to disk, then repeatedly merge the sorted runs using only a small in-memory buffer per run
Load the entire dataset into a compressed in-memory format and run standard quicksort on it
Use a hash table to store every element uniquely, then read them back out in sorted key order
External sorting is impossible; datasets that don't fit in memory cannot be sorted
questions.explanation: External merge sort applies the same divide-and-merge principle as in-memory merge sort, but at the granularity of disk-sized chunks: sortable-in-RAM runs are produced first, then merged in passes that only need to hold one buffered block per run in memory at a time, minimizing costly disk I/O relative to the amount of data processed.

questions.source_excerpt: GATE's CS Algorithms syllabus contrasts elementary sorting algorithms by swap/move count as a standard examinable topic; this item targets that general concept area rather than a specific transcribed exam question.
questions.question: Among bubble sort, selection sort, and insertion sort, which one performs the fewest element swaps or moves in the worst case on an array of n elements, and how many?
options: Selection sort, which performs at most n-1 swaps, one per pass, only when the pass finds a new minimum, regardless of the input's initial order
Bubble sort, which performs zero swaps in the worst case
Insertion sort, which never needs more than O(1) total shifts
All three always perform exactly the same number of swaps
questions.explanation: Selection sort only swaps once per outer-loop pass, placing the found minimum into position, giving at most n-1 swaps total no matter how the input is arranged, whereas bubble sort and insertion sort can each require up to Theta(n^2) swaps or shifts on a reverse-sorted array -- which is why selection sort is sometimes preferred when the cost of writing or swapping is much higher than the cost of comparing.
